explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but it's the opposite. Jehu says, “If you commanders wish to make me king, then do not let anyone escape from the city to go and tell it in Jezreel.” (2 Kings 9:15) He wants no warning going out. Nobody gets to run ahead and ring the doorbell for him.

Yes, it's the reverse of a warning. Jehu says, “…do not let anyone escape from the city to go and tell it in Jezreel.” (2 Kings 9:15) That's his instruction to the commanders. He doesn't want word going ahead to Jezreel.
That's him. The text says Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see Joram (2 Kings 9:16). Joram is laid up in Jezreel, so Ahaziah is basically visiting a patient. Jehu is about to crash that visit.

Good guess on the name, but it's not the visitor here. In this passage, Jehoshaphat is Jehu's father: “…Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi…” (2 Kings 9:14). The king who came down to see Joram is Ahaziah king of Judah (2 Kings 9:16). Easy to mix up when the names keep stacking like cookies on a rack.

Ben-hadad is called king of Aram elsewhere in Scripture (1 Kings 20:1), but he isn't in this passage. The king of Aram here is Hazael, the one Joram was fighting (2 Kings 9:15). The king who came to visit Joram in Jezreel is Ahaziah of Judah (2 Kings 9:16). That's a different crown from a different country.

Yes, that's the question. Joram tells his men, “Send him out to meet them and ask, ‘Have you come in peace?’…” (2 Kings 9:17) Simple question, but it's about to get a very strange answer. I think Joram expected a plain yes or no.
That's a smart thing to ask, but it's not what Joram says. He wants the rider to ask, “Have you come in peace?” (2 Kings 9:17) Nothing about names. The rider has one question to carry.

Counting heads is a fair idea, but Joram doesn't ask for it. The rider is sent to ask, “Have you come in peace?” (2 Kings 9:17) The watchman had only said he saw a company of troops. The king's question is about peace.

That's it. Jehu says, “What do you know about peace?” and then, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) Joram's rider came with a question about peace and got that answer. Then the watchman reports, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.” (2 Kings 9:18)

That would be the usual plan, but it's not what happens. Jehu says, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) The watchman then reports, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.” (2 Kings 9:18) So the king gets no answer from his rider.

Waiting by the road isn't what Jehu says. He tells the horseman, “Fall in behind me.” (2 Kings 9:18) That's an instruction to follow him, not to stay put. Then the watchman reports, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.” (2 Kings 9:18)

Yep. The watchman says the charioteer “…is driving like Jehu son of Nimshi…” (2 Kings 9:20). He recognizes the driving style from way up on that tower. I'd be nervous if somebody recognized my driving from that far away.
It's actually true. The watchman reports, “And the charioteer is driving like Jehu son of Nimshi…” (2 Kings 9:20). He doesn't say it's a stranger. He names Jehu from the tower.

explanations.answer: Rides out in his own chariot
explanations.explanation: Right. Joram shouts, “Harness!” and they harness his chariot (2 Kings 9:21). Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his own chariot. They meet Jehu on the property of Naboth the Jezreelite.

I get the thought, but the text doesn't say that. After the second horseman, Joram shouts, “Harness!” (2 Kings 9:21). Then he and Ahaziah set out, each in his own chariot. The king goes himself this time.

Shutting the gates is something a king might do, but the text doesn't mention it. What it says is that Joram shouts, “Harness!” and they harness his chariot (2 Kings 9:21). Then he and Ahaziah ride out to meet Jehu.

That's it. Jehu says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) Jezebel is Joram's mother. So Joram asks a yes or no question and gets a no, with a reason.

Joram does have the king of Judah riding beside him, but that isn't Jehu's answer. He says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) Jehu points at Jezebel, Joram's mother.

explanations.answer: The war with Hazael of Aram
explanations.explanation: The war with Hazael is in this story, since Joram was wounded in it (2 Kings 9:15). But it's not what Jehu names. He says, “How can there be peace… as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (2 Kings 9:22) His answer is about Jezebel.

Yes, he flees. Joram asks, “Have you come in peace, Jehu?” and Jehu answers about the idolatry and witchcraft of Joram's mother Jezebel (2 Kings 9:22). Then Joram turns around and flees, calling out, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” (2 Kings 9:23) I think that answer told him this was no friendly visit.
Nope, no attack from Joram. The text says he “…turned around and fled…” (2 Kings 9:23). He calls out a warning to Ahaziah as he goes. He's running, not fighting.
Surrender would mean staying put, and Joram doesn't. He turns around and flees, calling out, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” (2 Kings 9:23) He's trying to get away.

That's right. Jehu tells Bidkar his officer, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.” (2 Kings 9:25) This is heavy, so I'll say it plainly. Jehu ties it to what the LORD said about repaying on that plot of ground (2 Kings 9:26).

That's a natural guess, but Jehu doesn't say it. He tells Bidkar, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.” (2 Kings 9:25) That's where Jehu says the body should go. He says it's according to the word of the LORD (2 Kings 9:26).

A burial with his fathers is what happens to Ahaziah later (2 Kings 9:28). For Joram, Jehu says, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.” (2 Kings 9:25) That's a very different ending. Jehu says it's according to the word of the LORD (2 Kings 9:26).

Yes. Jehu says, “Now then, according to the word of the LORD, pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground.” (2 Kings 9:26) He points back to what the LORD declared about the blood of Naboth and his sons. The LORD's word is what Jehu points to.

It's true, friend. Jehu says, “Now then, according to the word of the LORD, pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground.” (2 Kings 9:26) He is pointing back to the LORD's word about repaying on that plot of ground. Jehu names the word of the LORD himself.

That's what he shouts. Jehu pursued him, shouting, “Shoot him too!” (2 Kings 9:27) The word too comes right after Joram was shot. Then they shot Ahaziah in his chariot on the Ascent of Gur, near Ibleam.
Jehu doesn't say that. He chases Ahaziah, shouting, “Shoot him too!” (2 Kings 9:27) There was no letting go on that road.
That would be a gentler chase, but the text doesn't say that. Jehu shouts, “Shoot him too!” (2 Kings 9:27) That's an order, not a rescue. The shot happens on the Ascent of Gur.

Right. His servants carried him by chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David (2 Kings 9:28). Before that, he fled to Megiddo and died there (2 Kings 9:27). Jerusalem is where his servants took him.
Samaria doesn't come up here. The text says his servants carried him to Jerusalem (2 Kings 9:28). He is buried with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David. Jerusalem is the city the text names.

Bethel isn't in this part of the story. His servants carried Ahaziah by chariot to Jerusalem (2 Kings 9:28). They buried him with his fathers in the City of David. The text names Jerusalem, not Bethel.

explanations.answer: Paints her eyes and watches from a window
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Jezebel “…painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She isn't hiding. I think she wanted to be seen.

explanations.answer: Hides in a room deep in the palace
explanations.explanation: That's what many people would do, but the text says something else. Jezebel “…painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She's up where Jehu can see her.

explanations.answer: Slips out of the city before dark
explanations.explanation: No sneaking out for her. The text says she “…painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.” (2 Kings 9:30) She stays right where Jehu can find her.
That's right. Jehu looks up at the window and calls out, “Who is on my side? Who?” (2 Kings 9:32) He repeats that one word, who. And two or three eunuchs look down.
It's true, friend. Jehu looked up at the window and called out, “Who is on my side? Who?” (2 Kings 9:32) The question he asks is who is on his side. Then two or three eunuchs looked down at him.
That's what Jehu yells: “Throw her down!” (2 Kings 9:33) I think this one hurts to read. The text says they threw her down.
That's not what Jehu says. He yells, “Throw her down!” (2 Kings 9:33) Bringing her to the gate isn't in the text. The text says plainly that they threw her down.
Jehu doesn't say that. He yells, “Throw her down!” (2 Kings 9:33) Keeping her inside isn't in the text. Then the text says they threw her down.
Yes, a king. Jehu says, “Take care of this cursed woman, and bury her, for she was the daughter of a king.” (2 Kings 9:34) That's his reason for the burial. It's a quiet line after a rough scene.
No priest in this line. Jehu says to bury her, “…for she was the daughter of a king.” (2 Kings 9:34) That's the reason he gives.
The text doesn't say prophet. Jehu says, “Take care of this cursed woman, and bury her, for she was the daughter of a king.” (2 Kings 9:34) The reason he gives is that she was a king's daughter.
That's not what they find. They went out to bury her, and the text says, “…they found nothing but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.” (2 Kings 9:35) Those parts are all they find.
Right, it's false. When they went out to bury her, “…they found nothing but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.” (2 Kings 9:35) That's all they find. Then they go back and tell Jehu.

That's him. Jehu says the LORD “…spoke through His servant Elijah the Tishbite…” (2 Kings 9:36). The text calls Elijah the LORD's servant. Jehu is saying what happened lines up with what the LORD said.
Nathan is called a prophet elsewhere (1 Kings 1:8), but he isn't named here. Jehu says the word was spoken “…through His servant Elijah the Tishbite…” (2 Kings 9:36). That's the name to remember.
Samuel isn't in this passage. Jehu says the LORD spoke “…through His servant Elijah the Tishbite…” (2 Kings 9:36). So the name to hold onto is Elijah.

Yes. The word through Elijah says, “…so that no one can say: This is Jezebel.” (2 Kings 9:37) That's how Jehu quotes it. Just before that line, the word says Jezebel's body will lie like dung in the field (2 Kings 9:37).

It's true. Jehu quotes the word of the LORD through Elijah: “…so that no one can say: This is Jezebel.” (2 Kings 9:37) That's the end of the line he quotes. It comes right after the word that her body will lie like dung in the field.
